About: the double-horned 21-cm line of a tilted rotating disc, and why its width measures vc sin i, not vc

About this simulation

On screen
Left: the gas disc in a fixed oblique view. It is tilted by i out of the dashed plane of the sky about its major axis. The view shows the disc axis, the arrow to the observer, the angle i, the azimuth φ of the bright tracer parcel and its vc arrow. Parcels are coloured by vr: blue at −300 km/s (towards), white at 0 and red at +300 km/s (away). Right, top: the 21-cm line, Fν scaled to its peak, against vr from −400 to +400 km/s. It carries ticks at ±vc sin i, the half-peak width W and a triangle that follows the tracer's vr. Right, bottom: the disc as the observer sees it, an ellipse of axis ratio cos i.
Controls
Inclination i sets the tilt, from 10° to 90° (edge on); the chips and the number box set it exactly. Circular speed vc sets the speed of the flat part of the rotation curve, from 100 to 300 km/s. Random gas motion σ runs from 5 to 25 km/s. Any change redraws the whole line at once. ▶ Play turns the disc once every 12 s at its rim. From a fresh start the line fills in over three turns.
Measured
The line, W and W/2 sin i come from the engine's exact 21-cm profile of a uniform disc with v = vc min(r/0.2R, 1), blurred by σ. W is the full width between the outermost half-peak points. cos i is the axis ratio of the image.
Readouts
In the sidebar under Controls: i and the image axis ratio cos i; the bright parcel’s vr, the edge speed vc sin i and the width W; and the inferred circular speed W/2 sin i.
Conditions
The gas is a thin, round, uniform disc on circular orbits, optically thin in the 21-cm line, with a flat rotation curve beyond 0.2 of its radius. cos i = b/a only for a thin round disc; real discs have thickness, and observers also correct W for the random motions before dividing by sin i.

Guided Inquiry

1 · One parcel of gas

Set the inclination to 90°, the circular speed to 200 km/s and the random gas motion to 10 km/s. Before pressing play, predict where on its circle the bright parcel has the largest radial velocity.

2 · The line from the whole disc

Keep the settings of question 1. Before pressing play, predict the shape of the line that fills in from the whole disc.

3 · Tilting the disc

Keep the circular speed at 200 km/s and the random gas motion at 10 km/s, and note the width W of about 414 km/s at an inclination of 90°. Before moving the slider, predict the width when the inclination is set to 30°.

4 · A slower disc seen edge-on

Keep the settings of question 3, with the inclination at 30° and the circular speed at 200 km/s. Before changing anything, predict the line when the circular speed is set to 100 km/s and the inclination to 90°.

5 · More random motion

Set the inclination to 60°, the circular speed to 200 km/s and the random gas motion to 5 km/s. Before moving the random-motion slider to 25 km/s, predict what happens to the horns.

6 · A nearly face-on disc

Set the inclination to 10°, the circular speed to 200 km/s and the random gas motion to 10 km/s. Before looking at the readouts, predict the inferred circular speed W/2 sin i.

7 · What the line width measures

A rotating disc gives a double-horned 21-cm line, and its width measures vc sin i, not vc: a fast disc seen nearly face-on and a slow one seen edge-on give the same line.

To recover vc, i must come from the image, cos i = b/a, which assumes a thin, round disc. The random motions add width that dividing by sin i magnifies, so the method works best for discs well away from face-on.

The 21-cm Line of a Tilted Disc

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

A disc of gas turns about its axis, and a radio telescope picks up the 21-cm line of its hydrogen. This sim tilts the disc and builds the line from every parcel of gas in it.

What you'll learn

  • How one parcel of gas sets a radial velocity.
  • How the whole disc builds the shape of the line.
  • How the line's width, the tilt and the speed are tied together.
  • How far the speed read off the line can be trusted.
The set-up (notes, Figure 92) at i = 60°: the disc is tilted by i out of the dashed plane of the sky. The dot is a parcel at azimuth φ, moving at vc.

What's on screen

  • Left, the turning disc. Parcels are coloured by vr: blue towards us (−300 km/s), red away (+300 km/s).
  • Orange dot: the bright parcel, with its vc arrow.
  • Top right, the 21-cm line: flux against vr, with tick marks, a width bar W and a triangle that follows the bright parcel.
  • Bottom right: the disc as the observer sees it, an ellipse of axis ratio b/a.
See itLook at the opening arrangement. Watch for: the disc edge-on, the line already drawn, and the width W and ticks marked on it.

03

One parcel: radial velocity vc sin i cos φ

Put a parcel at azimuth φ on the ring, measured in the disc from the major axis, the line where the disc meets the plane of the sky. It moves along the ring at vc, in the direction (−sin φ ê1 + cos φ ê2). The vector ê1 lies in the sky and has no part along the line of sight. The vector ê2 is tilted out of the sky by i, so it has a part sin i along it. The radial velocity is therefore:

Equation (8.9) of the notes. vc is the speed along the ring, i the inclination, φ the azimuth.

It is largest, vc sin i, where cos φ = ±1: at the two ends of the major axis, where the parcel moves straight along the line of sight. At φ = 90° and 270° the parcel is nearest to us or furthest from us, and it moves across the line of sight, so vr = 0.

Key idea. Only the part of the speed that points along the line of sight shows up as vr.
See itPress Play on the edge-on disc and follow the orange parcel. Watch for: the bright parcel vr swinging between +200 and −200 km/s once every 10.8 s (it sits at 0.9 of the radius, so it laps a little faster than the rim, which takes 12 s), and passing through 0 midway.
04

Two horns: the whole disc piles up at the edges of the line

Spread the gas evenly in azimuth round a flat rotation curve. The number of parcels per unit vr goes as 1/|dvr/dφ|, which the notes write as:

Gas per unit radial velocity, for a flat rotation curve and gas spread evenly in azimuth.

This is smallest at φ = 90°, where vr = 0, and large near φ = 0 and π, where vr approaches ±vc sin i. Equal steps in φ crowd together near the two ends of the vr axis, as the dots do below. The line has two horns near ±vc sin i, with a lower trough between them.

Parcels at equal steps of φ, dropped onto the vr axis: they crowd at the two ends.

In the sim the horns are blurred by σ and sit a little inside the edge. Edge-on, with vc = 200 and σ = 10 km/s, they peak near ±192 km/s and the trough is 0.33 of the peak. The gas inside 0.2R turns more slowly, so it adds to the trough.

See itLook at the line of the edge-on disc. Watch for: two tall peaks near ±200 km/s with a lower dip between them, the dip about a third of the peak.
05

Width W ≈ 2vc sin i, so vc = W / 2 sin i

The horns sit at ±vc sin i, so the full width between the two half-peak points is about twice that:

Equation (8.10). W is measured between the points where the flux falls to half its peak.

Blur pushes the half-peak points a little outwards, so W lies a little above 2vc sin i: at the opening settings W = 414 km/s against 400. The tilt has to come from the image. A thin, round disc at inclination i appears as an ellipse of axis ratio b/a = cos i (Problem 2 of the notes). With i known, the circular speed follows:

The speed worked out from the line, as in the notes. The sim's readout W/2 sin i.
W against i for vc = 200 and σ = 10 km/s, from the sim's own line profile. The dashed curve is 2vc sin i.
See itTip the disc to 30°. Watch for: W falling from 414 to 214 km/s, the edge speed reading 100 km/s, and b/a reading 0.87.
06

One line, two discs: the line fixes vc sin i, not vc and i

The profile depends on vc and i only through the product vc sin i. A disc with vc = 200 km/s at i = 30° and one with vc = 100 km/s edge-on both have vc sin i = 100 km/s: the same horns, the same trough and the same W = 214 km/s.

Two different discs, one line. Only the image tells them apart: b/a = cos 30° = 0.87, against 0.

That is why the notes take i from the shape of the image and not from the line. Since sin i ≤ 1, the line alone gives only W/2, a lower limit on vc.

Key idea. A narrow line can come from a slow disc or from a fast disc seen nearly face-on.
See itCompare a 200 km/s disc at 30° with a 100 km/s disc edge-on. Watch for: the line and the readouts matching, W = 214 km/s both times, while b/a changes from 0.87 to 0.00.
07

Random motion blurs the edges, and nearly face-on it inflates the speed

Random motion σ smears every parcel's vr. The horns round off and the trough fills, but the edges stay near ±vc sin i. At i = 60° and vc = 200 km/s, going from σ = 5 to 25 km/s moves the horns from ±169 to ±153 km/s, lifts the trough from 0.25 to 0.55 of the peak, and widens W only from 353 to 380 km/s.

At σ = 10 km/s the blur adds about 13–14 km/s to W at every tilt. Dividing by 2 sin i then multiplies it: by 1/2 edge-on, which gives 207 km/s, but by 1/0.347 at i = 10°. There W = 82 km/s, against 2vc sin i = 69 km/s, and the speed worked out from W comes to W/2 sin i = 237 km/s, for a true 200.

Key idea. The blur on W is nearly the same at every tilt, but the division by 2 sin i makes it count more as the disc turns face-on.

Observers also correct W for the random motions before dividing by sin i. The sim does not.

See itRaise σ from 5 to 25 km/s at i = 60°. Watch for: the horns lowering and rounding while W grows only a little, from 353 to 380 km/s.
See itNow tip the disc to 10°. Watch for: a narrow line, W = 82 km/s, and W/2 sin i reading 237 km/s although vc is still 200 km/s.
08

Where it matters: the Tully–Fisher distance ladder

In 1977 Tully and Fisher found that the luminosity of a spiral galaxy tracks its circular speed, L ∝ vc4 approximately, most tightly in the near infrared, where the galaxy's own dust hides little of the light. The notes derive that power from the virial theorem if spirals share one mass-to-light ratio and one mean surface brightness.

A measured W and an axis ratio give vc. The luminosity then follows, and with the measured flux it gives the distance d ∝ vc2 (8.14). So a speed that is too high by 18%, as at i = 10°, gives a distance too large by about 40%. The notes quote about 20% scatter in the distance of a single galaxy, and use the method out to about 100 Mpc.

The sim shows the notes' Figure 93: a flat rotation curve beyond an inner rise, gas spread over a disc, and a small random motion. It is not a fit to a named galaxy.

09

Summary

In one line. A turning, tilted gas disc gives a 21-cm line, and the line's shape, its width and the speed worked out from it depend on the tilt, the circular speed and the random motion of the gas.

Common mix-ups

  • "Tilting the disc does nothing, because the gas is still moving at vc." From i = 90° to 30°, W falls from 414 to 214 km/s.
  • "W is exactly 2vc sin i." At the opening settings the product is 400 km/s and W is 414: the extra is blur.
  • "Two identical lines mean two identical discs." A 200 km/s disc at 30° and a 100 km/s disc edge-on give the same line. Only the image differs.
  • "A face-on galaxy still gives vc if you divide carefully." At i = 10° the division gives 237 km/s for a true 200.

Things to try on your own

  • Set vc = 300 km/s, edge-on. W should read about 614 km/s.
  • Set i = 10° and σ = 25 km/s. The horns disappear into one hump, and W/2 sin i should read about 267 km/s.

The sim does not draw the notes' Faber–Jackson case for ellipticals.
